werk/hector-lavoe-la-voz.text:
La Voz was the first solo album by the singer Héctor Lavoe, released in 1975 on Fania Records. He had previously worked with Willie Colón, and Colón now produced and arranged this record as well. Rubén Blades sang in the backing chorus.

The album revolves around Lavoe's voice. Colón left out long percussion or instrumental solos so that the singing had all the room it needed. The opener El Todopoderoso and Mi Gente were the two big hits in Latin America and the United States. In Mi Gente, Ray Maldonado plays a trumpet solo. According to Allmusic, Lavoe stood out for his heavenly sound, and the record sounds warm and refined. Later critics regard the album as a high point of 1970s salsa and admire Lavoe's improvisations and expressive voice.
werk/hector-lavoe-la-voz.listen: Listen to El Todopoderoso and notice how Lavoe's voice stays in front, with the orchestra and percussion in the background.

werk/helen-reddy-long-hard-climb.text:
Long Hard Climb was released on 23 July 1973 on Capitol Records and is the fourth studio album by the Australian-American singer Helen Reddy. The producer was mainly Tom Catalano. The album consists mostly of songs aimed at the charts, but Reddy also ventured into New Orleans jazz in Lovin' You and into the English version of a new classic by Charles Aznavour, The Old Fashioned Way. It followed her 1972 album I Am Woman.

Delta Dawn was the first single. It spent twenty weeks on the Billboard Hot 100, one of them at number one. Leave Me Alone (Ruby Red Dress) followed in October and reached number three. The album itself rose to number eight in the United States and was certified gold in September 1973. In 2003 it appeared on CD for the first time, together with I Am Woman on a single disc.
werk/helen-reddy-long-hard-climb.listen: Listen to Lovin' You and notice how Reddy chooses a very different, lighter sound here than on the hit singles. Can you hear the influence of New Orleans?

werk/henry-mancini-combo.text:
Combo! is Henry Mancini's seventh studio album for RCA Victor. The album was recorded in Hollywood in June 1960 but was not released until early 1962. The sleeve notes argued that the small band, the combo, is too often forgotten in the golden decade of music from 1935 to 1945. The record aims to honour those ensembles with fresh jazz, partly written and partly improvised.

His task as arranger was to make eleven players sound like a full orchestra. He also used a harpsichord for a fresh sound. The players include Pete Candoli, Art Pepper and Shelly Manne. Billboard saw the album as a salute to the great pop combos of the past, with arrangements that swing.
werk/henry-mancini-combo.listen: Listen to Tequila and notice how big a sound eleven players can make together.

werk/henry-mancini-the-blues-and-the-bea.text:
The Blues and the Beat was the fourth album Henry Mancini made for RCA Victor, after the records built around Peter Gunn and The Mancini Touch. It was recorded in Hollywood in February 1960. In the sleeve notes Mancini wrote that jazz consists of two parts, the blues and the beat. The first side holds the bluesy numbers, the second the swinging ones.

For the blues numbers, four horns, trumpets and trombones provided a dark sound in Smoke Rings and Mood Indigo. On the beat side, Pete Candoli's trumpet drove Sing, Sing, Sing almost to a frenzy. Billboard praised the unusual instrumentation, but Ralph Gleason thought the record a gimmick. In 1961 the album won the first Grammy for Best Jazz Performance by a Large Group.
werk/henry-mancini-the-blues-and-the-bea.listen: Listen to Sing, Sing, Sing and notice how the arrangement builds slowly until the trumpet breaks loose.

werk/henry-mancini-the-mancini-touch.text:
The Mancini Touch was released in 1960 and shows Henry Mancini above all as an arranger and conductor. He works with an orchestra of some thirty-five players, including jazz soloists such as the drummer Shelly Manne and the vibraphonist Victor Feldman. Dick Peirce produced and Al Schmitt engineered.

The repertoire mixes original work with songs by others, such as Bijou by Ralph Burns and Like Young by Andre Previn. Greg Adams of Allmusic wrote that the soloists occasionally improvise within carefully crafted arrangements. In Bijou he already heard the sound of Baby Elephant Walk and The Pink Panther Theme passing by. Billboard praised the orchestra's sharpness and precision and the excellent stereo sound.
werk/henry-mancini-the-mancini-touch.listen: Listen to Bijou and notice how tightly the orchestra plays while still leaving room for a soloist.

werk/herbie-hancock-empyrean-isles.text:
Empyrean Isles is Herbie Hancock's fourth studio album, released in November 1964 on Blue Note. It was recorded on 17 June 1964 at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. Hancock plays piano, together with Freddie Hubbard, the bassist Ron Carter and the drummer Tony Williams. On this session Hubbard plays cornet instead of his usual trumpet. Alfred Lion produced.

All four tracks are original compositions, written over a period of two years. One of them, Cantaloupe Island, grew into a standard. The Penguin Guide to Jazz gave the album its maximum score of four stars. Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic wrote that the album officially established Hancock as an important artist in his own right.
werk/herbie-hancock-empyrean-isles.listen: Listen to Cantaloupe Island and notice how piano, cornet, bass and drums each have a place of their own.

werk/herbie-hancock-head-hunters.text:
After three experimental records with his Mwandishi sextet, Herbie Hancock wanted to make lighter music, with more of a foothold on earth. He put together a new group, the Headhunters, of which only the reed player Bennie Maupin came from the sextet. Bassist Paul Jackson and drummer Harvey Mason provided a relaxed funk feel. Hancock played all the synthesizers himself and chose the Hohner Clavinet instead of guitar. The recordings took place in San Francisco and the album was released in October 1973.

It contains four tracks. Watermelon Man was an old hit of Hancock's, reworked here, with Bill Summers blowing across a beer bottle and plenty of African percussion. Chameleon has a famous bass line, which Hancock played on an ARP Odyssey. The album brought jazz-funk to a wide audience, reached number thirteen on the American chart and for a time became the best-selling jazz album. Purists thought it a step too far, but its influence reached into funk, soul and hip hop.
werk/herbie-hancock-head-hunters.listen: In Chameleon, listen to the bass line that Hancock plays on a synthesizer, and notice how it carries the whole track.

werk/herbie-hancock-inventions-en-dimens.text:
Herbie Hancock recorded his third album for Blue Note on 30 August 1963. He plays piano, with the bassist Paul Chambers and the percussionists Willie Bobo and Chihuahua Martinez. It is a remarkable record: there is a great deal of Latin percussion, yet it is not Latin jazz. The album is above all a further exploration of modal jazz and post-bop.

All five tracks are his own. Triangle lasts well over eleven minutes and Succotash almost eight. In the 1970s the record was reissued under the title Succotash, with Hancock and Bobo on the cover and the sides reversed. The CD also includes a second version of Mimosa.
werk/herbie-hancock-inventions-en-dimens.listen: Listen to Succotash and notice the interplay between the piano and the two percussionists.

werk/herbie-hancock-maiden-voyage.text:
The pianist Ramsey Lewis recorded Maiden Voyage in 1968. The album was released on Cadet and ranked high on the American jazz and soul charts. Lewis plays piano, Cleveland Eaton bass and Maurice White drums. Charles Stepney wrote some of the tracks and made arrangements, as did Eaton.

The repertoire is varied. Lewis plays the title song by Herbie Hancock, but also Lady Madonna by The Beatles and Do You Know the Way to San Jose, known from Dionne Warwick. There are also songs by Bob Dylan, Aretha Franklin and Quincy Jones, alongside original pieces by Stepney and Eaton. In this way Lewis brought jazz, pop and soul together on one record, with his own trio as the constant foundation.
werk/herbie-hancock-maiden-voyage.listen: Listen to Lady Madonna and notice how Lewis turns the piano riff of a Beatles song into his own trio sound.

werk/herbie-hancock-my-point-of-view.text:
My Point of View is Herbie Hancock's second album and was released in 1963 on Blue Note. He stuck to hard bop and soul jazz and added a trombone to the trumpet and tenor sax on three tracks. For this he brought in Donald Byrd, Grachan Moncur III and Hank Mobley, and the guitarist Grant Green plays on two tracks. The drummer is the seventeen-year-old Tony Williams.

Two months after the sessions, Hancock and Williams joined Miles Davis's band, the later Second Great Quintet. According to Hancock, Blind Man, Blind Man evokes his background, after a blind guitarist in his neighbourhood in Chicago. In King Cobra he tried to widen the flow of the chords, in the modal style he used in 1965 on Maiden Voyage.
werk/herbie-hancock-my-point-of-view.listen: Listen to King Cobra and notice the space the band takes, with few chord changes.

werk/herbie-hancock-takin-off.text:
Takin' Off is Herbie Hancock's debut album, released in 1962 on Blue Note. Hancock plays piano with the tenor saxophonist Dexter Gordon, the trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, the bassist Butch Warren and the drummer Billy Higgins. All the tracks are his own. The record is a fine example of hard bop.

The bluesy Watermelon Man almost reached the top hundred of the singles charts and became a jazz standard. In 1973 Hancock made a funk version of it on Head Hunters. The record appeared on CD for the first time in 1996 and was reissued in 2007, remastered by Rudy Van Gelder.
werk/herbie-hancock-takin-off.listen: Listen to Watermelon Man and notice the bluesy theme and how the piano sets the tone in it.

werk/herman-brood-saturday-night.text: In 1978 Herman Brood and his band Wild Romance had a hit with Saturday Night. Brood was a pianist, a painter and the first real rock 'n' roll star of the Netherlands, who openly lived the way he sang, with drugs and scandals. In 1979 he tried to conquer America, without much success. His lifestyle ultimately proved fatal: in 2001 he jumped from the roof of the Hilton in Amsterdam.
werk/herman-brood-saturday-night.listen: Saturday Night is raw rock 'n' roll with piano. Listen for Brood's hoarse voice and the driving guitars.

werk/het-goede-doel-belgie.text: In 1982 Het Goede Doel, the Utrecht band around Henk Westbroek and Henk Temming, had a hit with België, synth-pop in Dutch. The chorus consists of questions that seem to be about nothing at all. After Doe Maar, dozens of Dutch-language bands followed within a few years. This is how Nederpop came into being in the sense the word usually has today: Dutch pop music in the Dutch language.
werk/het-goede-doel-belgie.listen: Listen for the synthesizers and the cool vocals, with a chorus full of questions.

werk/hikaru-utada-distance.text:
Distance is Hikaru Utada's third album and was released on 28 March 2001 on Toshiba EMI. It followed First Love, the best-selling record in Japanese music history. The songs were written between 1999 and 2001. For Addicted to You, the singer flew to Minneapolis in the summer of 1999 to produce with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. Time Limit came about with Rodney Jerkins. The rest of the record was made around the turn of the year, when the university was closed for a while.

The sound builds on R&B, with influences from hip hop, rock, reggae and techno. Wait & See is American R&B with funk and soul, Kettobase! is a fast pop-rock song and Parody has reggae touches. The title refers to the distances between people: in relationships, in dealings with one another and in feeling. AllMusic called Distance one of the most consistent and inventive albums in the body of work. The record topped the Oricon chart and broke the record for first-week sales.
werk/hikaru-utada-distance.listen: Listen to Wait & See -Risk- and notice the atmosphere: can you hear this American-flavoured R&B with a touch of funk and soul?

werk/hikaru-utada-first-love.text:
First Love is Hikaru Utada's first Japanese-language album and was released on 10 March 1999. The artist, born and raised in Manhattan, had earlier sung with their parents in the group U3 and recorded the English-language Precious in 1998. At the record company's request, the newcomer now wrote Japanese lyrics, with occasional English phrases in between. The year of recording took place mostly at weekends, because school came first. Their father Teruzane Utada and Akira Miyake co-produced, and Ted Jensen mixed the tracks in New York.

The album is R&B and dance-pop about love and relationships. Automatic opens the record, and Movin' on Without You is inspired by early 1990s dance. In My Room contains rap and scratches. Aaliyah's debut was an important source of inspiration. The record went straight to the top of the Oricon chart and is regarded as a milestone in the history of Japanese pop: one critic believed it changed the DNA of Japanese pop.
werk/hikaru-utada-first-love.listen: Listen to In My Room and notice the rap and the scratching: how do they give this R&B track a different character from an ordinary love song?

werk/hildur-gu-nadottir-mount-a.text:
Mount A is the debut album of the Icelandic musician Hildur Guðnadóttir. It was released in 2006 on 12 Tónar under the artist name Lost In Hildurness and was reissued, remastered, in 2010 by Touch, this time under her own name. The recordings took place in New York and in a house in Hólar, which was chosen for its good acoustics for cello.

The sound is a dark, somewhat repetitive soundscape. Hildur plays all the instruments herself: cello, viola da gamba, khuur, piano, zither, vibraphone and gamelan. The album has eleven pieces with short titles, from Light to You. Reflection lasts well over seven minutes, and You, the closing piece, more than ten.
werk/hildur-gu-nadottir-mount-a.listen: Listen to the longest piece, You, and try to hear which instruments you recognise: cello, piano, vibraphone or gamelan.

werk/hildur-gu-nadottir-without-sinking.text:
Without Sinking is the second solo album by the Icelandic cellist and composer Hildur Guðnadóttir. It was released in 2009 on the Touch label. Her previous record, Mount A from 2006, she had still released under the pseudonym Lost in Hildurness. Skúli Sverrisson, Jóhann Jóhannsson and her father Guðni Franzson play on this album. Valgeir Sigurðsson and Hildur herself mixed the recordings.

The ten tracks are calm and layered. Cello, zither, electronics and voice slide over one another. Pitchfork wrote that the tracks are as patient as they are graceful and that the voices move like tall grass in the wind. At the 2009 Kraumur Awards the album was among the six best records of the year. The magazine Fact placed it at number 32 on its list of the forty best albums of 2009.
werk/hildur-gu-nadottir-without-sinking.listen: Listen to Elevation, the opening track, and notice how the voices and the cello build up in layers. Try to hear where a new layer comes in.

werk/hooverphonic-a-new-stereophonic-sou.text:
Hooverphonic's debut album was released on 29 July 1996 on Columbia Records. The Belgian band was then still called Hoover, and the album appeared under that name. It is the only album with the singer Liesje Sadonius. Four singles came from the record: Wardrope, 2Wicky, Inhaler and Barabas. In 1997 an American release followed on Epic Records.

2Wicky contains a sample of Isaac Hayes's 1969 version of Walk On By, and a sample of Le Voile d'Orphée by Pierre Henry. Plus Profond was remade for the record because the original version contained a sample that could not be cleared. In 2011 a deluxe edition appeared as a box set, with the album on CD and LP, two CDs of remixes and rarities, and a book of essays by the band members.
werk/hooverphonic-a-new-stereophonic-sou.listen: In 2Wicky, listen for the sample of Walk On By by Isaac Hayes. Try to hear where it returns in the track.

werk/hooverphonic-blue-wonder-power-milk.text:
Blue Wonder Power Milk is the second album by the Belgian band Hooverphonic. It was released on 11 May 1998 on Columbia Records and is the first record with the singer Geike Arnaert. In August 1998 an American release followed on Epic Records. The photograph on the cover shows the interior of the Atomium in Brussels.

A writer for AllMusic called the record dream pop, indie pop and trip hop. According to him, the songs are interwoven with string arrangements and pulsing dance beats, which gives a sleepy feeling. Club Montepulciano, This Strange Effect, Eden and Lung were released as singles. Eden reached number 12 on the Walloon Ultratop.
werk/hooverphonic-blue-wonder-power-milk.listen: In Eden, listen to the strings and the beat. Notice whether you can hear the sleepy feeling that a reviewer says the record has.

werk/hooverphonic-hooverphonic-presents-.text:
This fourth album by Hooverphonic is a concept album about the fictional character Jackie Cane. She leaves her identical twin sister to become a professional singer. The pressure of fame almost drives her to madness. She stops performing and returns home to make amends, but her sister is bitter and poisons them both with a last supper.

The dreamlike atmosphere of earlier work remains in Nirvana Blue and Human Interest, which refers to Echoes by Pink Floyd. In The World Is Mine and Day After Day, critics hear the influence of Broadway. Sometimes contains a sample of Young Man Cried by The Walker Brothers. The record went platinum in Belgium and won two ZAMUs in 2002, for best pop group and best album. The World Is Mine became the theme tune of the TV series Mile High.
werk/hooverphonic-hooverphonic-presents-.listen: Listen to The World Is Mine, the first single. Notice the theatrical atmosphere, which is reminiscent of Broadway.

werk/hooverphonic-the-magnificent-tree.text:
The Magnificent Tree is the third album by the Belgian group Hooverphonic. It was released on 26 September 2000. The recording cost eight million Belgian francs, which made it one of the most expensive Belgian records, partly because the first three weeks were thrown away: according to the source, the group was heading in the wrong direction. The record company hoped for far higher sales than for the two earlier albums. Geike Arnaert sings, Raymond Geerts plays guitar and Alex Callier handles keyboards, bass, programming and production.

Four singles were released: Mad About You, Vinegar & Salt, Out of Sight and Jackie Cane. Vinegar & Salt contains a sample of Je Me Repose. Reactions were mixed. MTV thought the sound was becoming too modern, while AllMusic praised Arnaert's voice and called Out of Sight and Mad About You dramatic.
werk/hooverphonic-the-magnificent-tree.listen: Listen to Mad About You. Notice the strings and the voice of Geike Arnaert.

werk/horace-silver-horace-silver-trio.text:
This album was released in 1956 on Blue Note and collects recordings from 9 and 20 October 1952 and 23 November 1953. The pianist Horace Silver plays in a trio with the drummer Art Blakey. In 1952 the bassists are Gene Ramey and Curley Russell, in 1953 Percy Heath. In Mesage From Kenya, Sabu's conga joins in.

The sessions had previously been released on two 10-inch records: Introducing the Horace Silver Trio from 1952 and Horace Silver Trio and Art Blakey, Vol. 2 from 1953. The 12-inch LP left out four tracks from those records. The CD reissue contains all sixteen tracks from the original sessions. Alfred Lion was the producer, Rudy Van Gelder did the remastering and Leonard Feather wrote the sleeve notes.
werk/horace-silver-horace-silver-trio.listen: Listen to Mesage From Kenya and notice Sabu's conga alongside Art Blakey's drums.

werk/horace-silver-in-pursuit-of-the-27t.text:
In Pursuit of the 27th Man is a studio album by Horace Silver, released by Blue Note in 1973. The recordings were made on 6 October and 10 November 1972. The pianist plays together with the vibraphonist David Friedman, the trumpeter Randy Brecker and the tenor saxophonist Michael Brecker, with Bob Cranshaw on electric bass and Mickey Roker on drums. The line-up varies from session to session: we hear the Brecker brothers on three tracks, Friedman on four.

Scott Yanow gave the album four stars at AllMusic. He found the sound highly unusual for a record by this pianist, but the style remains, in his view, unmistakable: driving, melodic hard bop with a generous dose of funky soul.
werk/horace-silver-in-pursuit-of-the-27t.listen: Listen to Strange Vibes and notice David Friedman's vibraphone alongside the piano.

werk/horace-silver-silver-n-brass.text:
The pianist Horace Silver released this album in 1975 on Blue Note. He played with the trumpeter Tom Harrell, the tenor saxophonist Bob Berg, the bassists Ron Carter and Bob Cranshaw and the drummers Al Foster and Bernard Purdie. The recordings took place in January 1975 at A&R Studios in New York. A brass section was then added at Wally Heider Sound Studio III in Los Angeles, including Buddy Collette and Jerome Richardson. Wade Marcus wrote the arrangements.

There are tributes to Tadd Dameron in Dameron's Dance and to Duke Ellington in The Sophisticated Hippie. Even so, according to Scott Yanow of Allmusic the music is unmistakably that of the pianist: funky hard bop. He gave the album three stars.
werk/horace-silver-silver-n-brass.listen: Listen to Dameron's Dance and notice how the added brass makes the small group sound bigger.

werk/horace-silver-silver-n-wood.text:
The pianist Horace Silver recorded this album on 7 November 1975 at A&R Studios in New York, with the trumpeter Tom Harrell, the tenor saxophonist Bob Berg, the bassist Ron Carter and the drummer Al Foster. On 2 and 3 January 1976 a brass section was added in Los Angeles, under the direction of Wade Marcus. Those playing in it included Buddy Collette, Jerome Richardson, Lanny Morgan, Jack Nimitz, Garnett Brown and Frank Rosolino. The album was released on Blue Note.

The record consists of two long suites of four parts each, The Tranquilizer Suite and The Process Of Creation Suite, each taking up an entire side. Scott Yanow of Allmusic did not find the suites very memorable, but praised the strong solos and called the music typical hard bop. He gave the album three stars.
werk/horace-silver-silver-n-wood.listen: Listen to Keep On Gettin' Up, the first part of The Tranquilizer Suite, and notice the solos above the added brass.

werk/howlin-wolf-howlin-wolf.text:
This 1962 album is really a compilation. Chess collected twelve singles that the Chicago bluesman had released between June 1957 and December 1961, almost all written by Willie Dixon. The producer was Ralph Bass. Because of the drawing of a rocking chair on the cover, the record is also known as The Rockin' Chair Album.

The record features tracks such as The Red Rooster, Spoonful and Back Door Man, with the singer's raw voice, guitar and harmonica, and accompaniment from, among others, Hubert Sumlin and Otis Spann. Rolling Stone described the collection as an outrageous set of songs about sex. Its influence reached far. Sam Cooke and the Rolling Stones made their own versions of Little Red Rooster, Cream recorded Spoonful, the Doors played Back Door Man and Led Zeppelin used lines from Back Door Man in Whole Lotta Love. In 1985 the record won a Blues Music Award as a classic.
werk/howlin-wolf-howlin-wolf.listen: Listen to The Red Rooster and notice how the heavy, raw voice and the sharp guitar together create a menacing atmosphere.

werk/hugh-masekela-grrr.text:
Grrr is Hugh Masekela's second studio album. It was recorded in New York and released in 1966 on Mercury Records. Ed Townsend produced. Masekela arranged nine of the ten tracks and Jonas Gwangwa one. They are short instrumental pieces in which jazz meets mbaqanga, the rhythmically complex South African music.

Some of the accompaniment is not credited on the sleeve: in his autobiography Masekela names, among others, Eric Gale on guitar, Larry Willis on piano, Morris Goldberg on saxophone and Howard St. John on tuba. A reviewer for Dusty Groove wrote that the sound is less polished than on later hits, with sparse tracks, dancing piano lines and a raw, soulful trumpet.
werk/hugh-masekela-grrr.listen: Listen to Ntjilo Ntjilo and notice how the trumpet plays over the sparse accompaniment.

werk/hugh-masekela-the-americanization-o.text:
This live album was recorded in November 1965 at the nightclub The Village Gate in New York and released in June 1966 on MGM. It mixes American jazz themes with traditional South African influences. The president of MGM thought Hugh Masekela's records too African for American taste, after which the trumpeter moved to Chisa and Blue Thumb.

AllMusic hears the influence of Dizzy Gillespie and Freddie Hubbard, and John Coltrane as an inspiration in Myxolydia. Masekela called the core of the sound township bop: short trumpet bursts that sometimes lean towards microtonality. The repertoire is largely South African, with two songs by his wife at the time, Miriam Makeba. The opener Bajabula Bonke appeared here on record for the first time.
werk/hugh-masekela-the-americanization-o.listen: In Bajabula Bonke (Healing Song), listen to how the track begins quietly and softly and gradually builds.

werk/hugh-masekela-trumpet-africaine.text:
Trumpet Africaine: The New Beat from South Africa is the first studio album by the South African musician Hugh Masekela. It was recorded in New York and released in August 1962 on Mercury Records, when he was still at school. He plays flugelhorn and trumpet and sings. Hugo Montenegro provided the arrangements and conducted.

A reviewer for Dusty Groove observed that the jazz element on the record is strong and that all the musicians play with vitality. This makes the album sound fresh and sets it sharply apart from the rest of the trumpeter's early records. The subtitle shows what it was all about: a new beat from South Africa.
werk/hugh-masekela-trumpet-africaine.listen: In Click Song, listen to the lively interplay between the soloist and the accompaniment.

werk/ice-cube-amerikkka-s-most-wanted.text:
After a bitter break with N.W.A and Ruthless Records, Ice Cube immediately began work on a solo record. He wanted Dr. Dre as producer, but that did not happen. He therefore worked with Sir Jinx, and then in New York with Public Enemy's production team, the Bomb Squad. He came into the studio with notebooks full of rhymes. The album was released on 16 May 1990 on Priority Records.

The lyrics are about life in the ghettos of Los Angeles: drugs, racism and poverty. The title song parodies the television programme America's Most Wanted, and on Endangered Species (Tales From the Darkside) Chuck D raps along. In It's a Man's World, Cube engages in a war of words with Yo-Yo. Critical opinion was divided: some found the lyrics repellent, others praised the sharp tone. Later, many critics saw the album as a hip hop classic that influenced many rappers.
werk/ice-cube-amerikkka-s-most-wanted.listen: Listen to Endangered Species (Tales From the Darkside) and notice how the hard beats of the Bomb Squad go together with the voices of Ice Cube and Chuck D.

werk/ice-cube-death-certificate.text:
Death Certificate is Ice Cube's second studio album and was released on 29 October 1991 on Priority Records. He wrote and recorded it from late 1990, while also contributing to records by Yo-Yo and Del tha Funkee Homosapien and making his film debut in Boyz n the Hood. The producers were Sir Jinx, DJ Pooh and Cube himself. The sound is more West Coast than on its predecessor, with plenty of 1970s funk and soul.

The album is divided into two halves, The Death Side and The Life Side. The first describes violence and drugs, the second looks ahead. With True to the Game and above all No Vaseline, Cube responds to his former group N.W.A. Black Korea caused a great deal of controversy, and in Great Britain this track and No Vaseline were at first removed from the record. Critics were full of praise, and The Source later gave the album its highest rating.
werk/ice-cube-death-certificate.listen: Listen to No Vaseline and notice how Ice Cube addresses the members of his former group one by one.

werk/ice-cube-lethal-injection.text:
Lethal Injection is Ice Cube's fourth studio album. It was released on 7 December 1993 on Priority Records. The producers included QDIII, Madness 4 Real, Sir Jinx and Laylaw, and the rapper co-produced himself. Three singles were released: Really Doe, You Know How We Do It and Bop Gun (One Nation), a track with a Funkadelic sample that was shown often on MTV. Down for Whatever became known through the 1999 film Office Space.

Critical opinion was divided. Some felt that he was adapting to gangsta rap and dealing with fewer social themes than on earlier records. The lyrics were also criticised as anti-police, racist and misogynistic. Over the years the appreciation of the album has grown.
werk/ice-cube-lethal-injection.listen: Listen to Bop Gun (One Nation), on which George Clinton sings along. Notice how the funk of Funkadelic lies beneath the track.

werk/ice-cube-the-predator.text:
The Predator is Ice Cube's third studio album and was released on 17 November 1992. It came out a few months after the Los Angeles riots of that year, and many tracks are about the tensions between black and white in the United States. In We Had to Tear This Mothafucka Up he addresses the officers who walked free in the Rodney King case, and Who Got the Camera? shows how a black man is beaten by the police. The title refers in part to the film Predator 2, from which the album uses samples.

The singles were It Was a Good Day, Check Yo Self and Wicked. Now I Gotta Wet'cha gave rise to the expression It's on like Donkey Kong. The album received good reviews and, on release, stood at number one on the Billboard 200.
werk/ice-cube-the-predator.listen: Listen to It Was a Good Day and notice how the lyrics describe an ordinary day, on an album full of heavier themes.

werk/ice-t-o-g-original-gangster.text:
Ice-T recorded his fourth album between July 1990 and January 1991 in Los Angeles, and it was released in May 1991 on Sire Records. Seven producers worked on it, including Afrika Islam and DJ Aladdin, and the rapper himself was executive producer. Guests included Body Count and artists from his own Rhyme Syndicate. The CD had 24 tracks, the LP only 16.

The record contains raw stories about a crumbling American society, with humour and sometimes bitterness too. NME praised it as his best effort to date. Escape from the Killing Fields rewrites Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos by Public Enemy and explains the original metaphor. The Tower stands out as sad and booming. There are also critical voices: Select felt that the record works better as a manifesto than as music. In America the album went gold, and many people regard it as his best.
werk/ice-t-o-g-original-gangster.listen: Listen to The Tower: notice the heavy, booming sound that suits the sad mood of the track.

werk/ike-en-tina-turner-dynamite.text:
Dynamite! was the second studio album by Ike & Tina Turner and was released in May 1962 on Sue Records. The duo was busy performing on the Chitlin' Circuit and with club residencies in their home base of St. Louis. In between, they recorded new material, and some of the tracks come from the sessions of 1961 and 1962. The album also includes hits from their debut album, such as A Fool in Love and I Idolize You.

It's Gonna Work Out Fine became their second million-seller and earned their first Grammy nomination. On that track Mickey & Sylvia play guitar and sing along. Won't You Forgive Me is a pop-soul ballad, a duet between Ike and Tina. Letter from Tina appears here in its entirety for the first time. Poor Fool, Tra La La La La and You Should'a Treated Me Right also reached the Billboard Hot 100. A reviewer in 1962 praised the alternation between quiet numbers and fiery excitement.
werk/ike-en-tina-turner-dynamite.listen: Listen to A Fool in Love and notice Tina Turner's vocals and how the band accompanies her voice.

werk/illinois-jacquet-desert-winds.text:
The saxophonist Illinois Jacquet recorded Desert Winds in 1964 with the guitarist Kenny Burrell. The album was released on Argo. Jacquet plays tenor and alto saxophone and Burrell electric guitar. Also playing are Tommy Flanagan on piano, Wendell Marshall on bass, Ray Lucas on drums and Willie Rodriguez on congas.

The repertoire mixes standards and original work: When My Dreamboat Comes Home, Star Eyes, Lester Leaps In by Lester Young and Blues for the Early Bird by Jacquet himself. The title song is by Esmond Edwards. AllMusic gave the album three and a half stars and called it underrated and modest, full of easy charm, without dazzling solos but with plenty of calm, lyrical moments.
werk/illinois-jacquet-desert-winds.listen: Listen to Lester Leaps In, the longest track on the album, and notice the calm, lyrical tone of the solos.

werk/illinois-jacquet-swing-s-the-thing.text:
In late 1956 the American tenor saxophonist Illinois Jacquet recorded this album for the Clef label. He plays in a sextet with the trumpeter Roy Eldridge, the pianist Jimmy Jones, the guitarist Herb Ellis, the bassist Ray Brown and the drummer Jo Jones. All six are experienced musicians, and you can hear it in the space between them.

The album has six tracks of between four and almost seven minutes. It includes jazz standards such as Can't We Be Friends?, Have You Met Miss Jones? and Lullaby of the Leaves, alongside Harlem Nocturne. Las Vegas Blues was written by Eldridge and Achtung by Jacquet himself. The music leans on long solos. Thom Jurek of AllMusic wrote that the magic lies in the performances, with so many great names together, and called it essential Jacquet.
werk/illinois-jacquet-swing-s-the-thing.listen: Listen to Harlem Nocturne and notice how the tenor saxophone gives the melody of this track space and warmth.

werk/incognito-100-and-rising.text:
100° and Rising was released in 1995 on Talkin' Loud Records and is the fifth album by the British acid jazz band Incognito. Bandleader Jean-Paul Bluey Maunick produced it himself and plays guitar on almost all the tracks. Gilles Peterson handled the A&R. Many guests worked on the record, such as horn players, strings under the direction of Simon Hale and several singers, including Joy Malcolm and Pamela Y. Anderson.

The band mixes jazz, soul and funk. Two singles were released, I Hear Your Name and Everyday, and Everyday reached the British chart. AllMusic called the band smooth, capable and profound: there is little new compared with earlier records, but the group finds new variations on its own sound. Rolling Stone praised the carefully constructed melodies and Maunick's sensual production.
werk/incognito-100-and-rising.listen: Listen to Everyday and notice how vocals, horns and rhythm section together create a smooth groove.

werk/incognito-positivity.text:
Positivity was released in 1993 and is the album by the British band Incognito, who supported the record with a tour of North America. Bandleader Jean-Paul Maunick, nicknamed Bluey, produced it himself. He drew his inspiration mainly from Talking Book and Innervisions by Stevie Wonder. You can hear this in the funk grooves, the tight horn section and the smooth, jazzy arrangements, in which the singers Maysa Leak and Mark Anthoni are given plenty of room. There is more singing than on the two earlier albums.

The reviews were positive. The Washington Post praised the imagination and the power of the horns, and The Atlanta Journal-Constitution counted the record among the best R&B albums of 1994. AllMusic called the mix of bebop, soul, classical and dance exemplary. MusicHound R&B called Deep Waters an important acid jazz track.
werk/incognito-positivity.listen: Listen to Deep Waters and notice how groove, vocals and horns together build a warm, jazzy atmosphere that is also very danceable.

werk/iq-nomzamo.text:
Nomzamo is the third studio album by the British neo-prog band IQ and was released in April 1987. The band recorded it from January to February 1987 at Chipping Norton Recording Studios in Oxfordshire, under the direction of the producer Ken Thomas. It was the first record without the singer Peter Nicholls, who had been replaced by P.L. Menel.

The band otherwise consisted of the guitarist Mike Holmes, the bassist Tim Esau, the keyboard player Martin Orford and the drummer Paul Cook. A saxophonist and a few backing singers also play on the record, and Jules O'Kine sings a duet in Colourflow. Part of the recording was done in Kingston, Jamaica. The album was released through Squawk Records and distributed internationally by Mercury, in the United Kingdom by Vertigo and in West Germany by Metronome.
werk/iq-nomzamo.listen: Listen to No Love Lost and notice how the new singer P.L. Menel gives the band a different voice.

werk/iron-maiden-killers.text:
Killers is Iron Maiden's second studio album, released on 16 February 1981 on EMI. It was the first with the guitarist Adrian Smith and the producer Martin Birch, and the last with the singer Paul Di'Anno. Steve Harris wrote almost everything. Many of the songs date from the years before the debut: Wrathchild and Innocent Exile are among the first songs Harris ever wrote. Murders In the Rue Morgue is based on a story by Edgar Allan Poe, and it is the band's only album with two instrumentals. According to Harris, the production was very different from that of the debut.

The first reactions were mixed, and Sounds gave it one star. Later the record gained more appreciation. Steve Huey of AllMusic called the guitar duo of Smith and Dave Murray the strongest in heavy metal, and Metal Hammer saw the album as an important transition to what came next.
werk/iron-maiden-killers.listen: Listen to Wrathchild and follow Steve Harris's bass line: on this album the bass and the guitar duo are clearly audible in the mix.

werk/iron-maiden-piece-of-mind.text:
In December 1982 the drummer Clive Burr left the band and Nicko McBrain, formerly of the French band Trust, took his place. Iron Maiden then withdrew to Jersey to write, rehearsing in the restaurant of a hotel that stood empty out of season. The fourth album was recorded in the Bahamas, at Compass Point Studios in Nassau. The mixing followed at Electric Lady Studios in New York.

The lyrics often come from books and films. To Tame a Land is about the novel Dune, Where Eagles Dare about the war film, and The Trooper about a poem by Tennyson. For Still Life the band hid a message that you can only hear if you play the record backwards: a joke aimed at the critics who called them satanic. The album reached number three on the British chart and mostly received good reviews.
werk/iron-maiden-piece-of-mind.listen: Listen to The Trooper and notice how the lyrics tell a story about a battle. Hear how the music follows that story.

werk/iron-maiden-powerslave.text:
After the Piece of Mind tour, Iron Maiden wrote the songs for Powerslave in 1984 in a hotel on Jersey. The recording followed from February to June at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas. It was the group's first album with the same line-up as the previous record. The cover and the accompanying World Slavery Tour took on an Ancient Egyptian theme, drawn from the title track.

The lyrics often come from films, books and history. Aces High is about the Battle of Britain and 2 Minutes to Midnight about the tension of the Cold War. Powerslave is narrated by a pharaoh who wonders why he has to die. The closing track Rime of the Ancient Mariner is an adaptation of the poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge and lasts almost fourteen minutes. The album entered the British chart at number two. The accompanying tour also went behind the Iron Curtain.
werk/iron-maiden-powerslave.listen: Listen to Rime of the Ancient Mariner and notice how, in almost fourteen minutes, the track acts out the story of Coleridge's poem, with passages from the text itself.

werk/iron-maiden-somewhere-in-time.text:
After the exhausting World Slavery Tour of 1984 and 1985, which lasted 331 days, the band was given four months' rest. The guitarists and the bassist used that time to experiment with new equipment. The result was a different sound: for the first time, guitar and bass synthesizers were used. The singer Bruce Dickinson wrote nothing this time, because his songs were rejected. It is precisely the tracks by the guitarist Adrian Smith that stand out.

The recording was expensive and spread across three countries: bass and drums in the Bahamas, guitars and vocals in Hilversum, the mix in New York. Themes such as space and time recur, although the band did not intend a concept album. Caught Somewhere in Time is narrated by the devil, Wasted Years is about homesickness while touring. The reviews were mostly positive, and Metal Hammer called it the most underrated Iron Maiden album of the 1980s.
werk/iron-maiden-somewhere-in-time.listen: Listen to Wasted Years and notice how the track is about homesickness and alienation. Hear how the music fits that.

werk/iron-maiden-the-number-of-the-beast.text:
With The Number of the Beast, a new phase began for Iron Maiden in 1982. It was the first album with the singer Bruce Dickinson and the last with the drummer Clive Burr. The producer Martin Birch felt that the previous singer could not handle Steve Harris's complicated direction. For the first time the band made an album from scratch, which meant that recording and mixing had to be finished in just five weeks. Stories went round about Battery Studios, about lights that switched themselves on and off and equipment that failed.

The singles were Run to the Hills and The Number of the Beast. The first became the band's first top-ten hit in England. The album reached the top spot on the British album chart. It also caused an uproar, especially in the United States, because of the lyrics of the title track and the cover by Derek Riggs, on which Eddie controls Satan like a puppet. Since then the band has carried the nickname The Beast.
werk/iron-maiden-the-number-of-the-beast.listen: Listen to Run to the Hills and notice the voice of Bruce Dickinson, who was making his first album with the band here. Hear how his singing carries the chorus.

werk/irving-berlin-alexander-s-ragtime-b.text: In 1911 Irving Berlin wrote Alexander's Ragtime Band, a cheerful song about a band that plays ragtime. The sheet music sold more than a million copies. Berlin had come to New York from Russia as a child, could not read music and played the piano on the black keys. Even so, he became one of the most successful songwriters of the century, with songs such as White Christmas and God Bless America.
werk/irving-berlin-alexander-s-ragtime-b.listen: This is Louis Armstrong's version from 1937. Hear how he breathes new life, with swing, into a song more than twenty years old.

werk/irving-berlin-white-christmas.text: On 29 May 1942 in Los Angeles, Bing Crosby recorded White Christmas, a song by Irving Berlin for the film Holiday Inn, in about eighteen minutes. In the middle of the Second World War, many Americans longed for home, and the song struck that chord. It became the best-selling single ever, with an estimated fifty million copies or more. One well-written song could give a writer an income for life.
werk/irving-berlin-white-christmas.listen: Listen for Crosby's calm, warm voice, which is almost spoken. This soft style of singing close to the microphone is called crooning.

werk/isaac-hayes-black-moses.text:
Black Moses is a double album from 1971 on Enterprise, the Stax label, and the fifth studio album by Isaac Hayes. It came out after his successful Shaft. The title comes from the nickname given to him by the Stax director Dino Woodward. Hayes at first found it disrespectful, but later saw it as a symbol of black pride. The cover unfolds into a poster on which he appears as Black Moses.

There are many cover versions, such as Never Can Say Goodbye by the Jackson 5, which reached number 22 on the Billboard Hot 100, and (They Long To Be) Close To You by The Carpenters. Hayes called it one of his most personal works. Ike's Rap II was widely sampled, by Portishead among others.
werk/isaac-hayes-black-moses.listen: Listen to Never Can Say Goodbye and notice how the Jackson 5 song takes on a character of its own here.

werk/isaac-hayes-hot-buttered-soul.text:
Isaac Hayes's first solo album sold poorly for Stax. He was about to return to his work behind the scenes as a producer and songwriter when, in 1968, the label lost its entire catalogue after the break with Atlantic. The label boss Al Bell had all the artists record new work. Hayes demanded complete creative control for a second record, and got it.

He recorded the album in Memphis with the Bar-Kays, played Hammond organ and sang live while conducting the band. Strings and horns were added later in Detroit, for a full orchestral sound beneath the rhythm section. There are only four long tracks on it, including a twelve-minute version of Walk On By and one of almost nineteen minutes of By the Time I Get To Phoenix. The album topped the R&B chart, received glowing reviews and is regarded as a milestone in soul.
werk/isaac-hayes-hot-buttered-soul.listen: In Walk On By, listen to how the track is slowly stretched out, and to Harold Beane's guitar solo.

werk/isaac-hayes-presenting-isaac-hayes.text:
Presenting Isaac Hayes was in 1968 the first release on Enterprise, a new Stax label. He had been working for Stax for years as a songwriter, producer and session musician. To keep Al Bell happy he recorded an album as a jazz trio, together with Al Jackson Jr. and Donald Duck Dunn of Booker T. & the MGs. No material had been prepared, so the three improvised an album together. It has therefore been called a jam session on record.

Precious, Precious was recorded as a nineteen-minute piece and cut down to under three minutes for the single. Single and album did little commercially. He then had to make a new album, and that became Hot Buttered Soul. After that success, Atlantic reissued the record as In the Beginning. The Rolling Stone Album Guide calls it a bluesy after-hours jam session.
werk/isaac-hayes-presenting-isaac-hayes.listen: In Medley: I Just Want To Make Love To You/Rock Me Baby, listen to how piano, bass and drums, just the three of them, take up the space and follow one another.

werk/isaac-hayes-the-isaac-hayes-movemen.text:
The Isaac Hayes Movement is Isaac Hayes's third studio album and was released in April 1970, as the successor to Hot Buttered Soul. The name comes from Marvell Thomas, who named the backing group after the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Like the previous record, the album has only four long tracks with extended orchestral arrangements, this time all covers of other people's work. I Stand Accused by Jerry Butler begins with a spoken introduction of almost five minutes, and on Something by The Beatles John Blair plays violin.

The album spent seven weeks at the top of the soul albums chart and reached number 8 on the Billboard 200.
werk/isaac-hayes-the-isaac-hayes-movemen.listen: Listen to I Stand Accused and notice the long spoken introduction before the song itself begins.

werk/isaac-hayes-to-be-continued.text:
...To Be Continued is Isaac Hayes's fourth studio album. It was released in 1970 on Enterprise, the Stax label. On earlier records he had already covered songs by Burt Bacharach and Hal David: Walk On By on Hot Buttered Soul and I Just Don't Know What to Do With Myself on The Isaac Hayes Movement.

This album also features a Bacharach and David song, namely The Look of Love. A shortened version was released as a single and reached number 79 on the Billboard Hot 100. The album itself did better: it topped the Billboard charts for Black Albums and Jazz Albums and reached number 11 on the Billboard 200.
werk/isaac-hayes-to-be-continued.listen: In The Look of Love, listen to how a well-known song by Burt Bacharach and Hal David sounds in a version of its own here: which parts do you recognise from the original song, and what is different?

werk/j-dilla-donuts.text:
Donuts was released on 7 February 2006, J Dilla's 32nd birthday and three days before his death. He had been ill since 2002 with a rare blood disease, later also developed lupus and was often in hospital. The best-known version of the story says that he made the record at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, with a portable turntable and a sampler. The writer Dan Charnas tells a different version in his book Dilla Time: the record began at home as a beat tape and was largely finished by Jeff Jank of Stones Throw.

The album is instrumental and runs like an endless loop: the last track flows into the first. The 31 short tracks use 34 samples from rock, jazz and soul. Critics praised the dense, idiosyncratic samples and the way the record seems to look mortality in the eye. In 2020 Rolling Stone placed it at number 386 on its list of the 500 best albums.
werk/j-dilla-donuts.listen: Listen to Last Donut of the Night and then straight away to Donuts (Outro): can you hear how the end flows seamlessly into the beginning?

werk/j-dilla-jay-love-japan.text:
Jay Love Japan is J Dilla's fourth studio album and his second posthumous project. He began it, and possibly finished it, before his death in February 2006. It was intended as an instrumental EP with two guest tracks. The release was chaotic: promo versions circulated, a Japanese release from 2006 is now regarded as a promo, and the announced release dates were missed several times. On 26 June 2007 the album appeared on the iTunes Store, and in 2008 the label Operation Unknown distributed it in shops.

In 2016 the album came out on CD and LP via Dilla's estate and Vintage Vibez Music Group, remastered and in the right order, with eleven tracks in twenty-five minutes. The tracks are built on soul and pop samples: Yesterday uses Gladys Knight & the Pips, Say It The Emotions and Can't You See Diana Ross & the Supremes. Can't You See is accompanied by a series of videos.
werk/j-dilla-jay-love-japan.listen: Listen to Yesterday, a short track of just over a minute, built on a sample of Gladys Knight & the Pips.

werk/j-dilla-the-shining.text:
The Shining is J Dilla's third studio album, released on 22 August 2006 on BBE Records. He died on 10 February 2006 and the album was not yet finished at that time. The producer Karriem Riggins finished it for his mother and, according to the source, also at the request of its maker himself; it was about 75 per cent complete. During his treatment at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center he worked on both Donuts and this album, with a Boss SP-303 and a small record player for singles.

Guests include Common, Busta Rhymes, D'Angelo, Madlib and Black Thought. The closing track Won't Do is the only track on which he raps alone. So Far to Go is a vocal version of Bye from Donuts, intended as a remix of Go! by Common. The reviews were generally positive. An instrumental version followed shortly after the album.
werk/j-dilla-the-shining.listen: Listen to Won't Do, the closing track, and notice that here he alone raps, without guests.

werk/j-dilla-welcome-2-detroit.text:
Welcome 2 Detroit is J Dilla's first studio album and was released on 26 February 2001. It came after Fantastic, Vol. 2 by his group Slum Village and opened BBE's Beat Generation series, albums in which the producer takes centre stage. The cover credits both Jay Dee and J Dilla: it was the first time he officially used the name J Dilla.

The album showcases talent from his home town. Elzhi can be heard on Come Get It and Phat Kat on Featuring Phat Kat. The sound ranges from gritty hardcore hip hop in Pause to electronic psychedelia in B.B.E. Rico Suave Bossa Nova is inspired by the Brazilian group Azymuth, with a rhythm by Karriem Riggins. He sings the lead vocal himself on Think Twice, a cover of Donald Byrd, and replays all the instruments on African Rhythms. In the closing track One he thanks the people who helped him in hip hop.
werk/j-dilla-welcome-2-detroit.listen: Listen to African Rhythms and notice that all the instruments have been replayed here, including the spoken introduction of the original.

werk/j-j-johnson-blue-trombone.text:
Blue Trombone was released in 1957 on Columbia Records. It is an early example of hard bop. The trombonist J.J. Johnson plays here with the pianist Tommy Flanagan, the bassist Paul Chambers and the drummer Max Roach.

Alongside Johnson's own pieces, such as Kev, Blue Trombone and 100 Proof, the quartet plays standards such as Hello Young Lovers, What's New and Gone With the Wind. The title piece is a single recording, but on the original LP it is split across two sides. The split falls exactly at the start of Chambers's bass solo. The album was later also released on CD, in 1994 on Tristar. Michael Nastos of AllMusic gave it four stars. According to him, the music shows why Johnson was regarded as the best jazz trombonist of bop and post-bop.
werk/j-j-johnson-blue-trombone.listen: In Blue Trombone, listen to Paul Chambers's bass solo: on the LP, the second side of the piece began there.

werk/jack-bruce-harmony-row.text:
Harmony Row is Jack Bruce's third studio album, released in July 1971. The title refers to a street in Glasgow, close to where he grew up. The cover was shot at the row of houses in Govan. The recording took place at Command Studios in London, in January 1971, with Chris Spedding on guitar and John Marshall on drums.

Vocals, guitars and drums were recorded at the same time on each track, with a live feel. Spedding later spoke of the tension in the studio: some tracks were challenging and everyone wanted to play them without mistakes. Bruce later called it his favourite solo album, although it did not chart on release. The single The Consul at Sunset is inspired by the novel Under the Volcano by Malcolm Lowry.
werk/jack-bruce-harmony-row.listen: Listen to The Consul at Sunset and notice how vocals, guitar and drums play together like a band.

werk/jack-bruce-out-of-the-storm.text:
Out of the Storm is Jack Bruce's fourth studio album, released in 1974, after the end of Cream and of West, Bruce and Laing. On the advice of the engineer Andy Johns it was recorded largely in Los Angeles and San Francisco, with American session musicians such as Steve Hunter on guitar and Jim Keltner and Jim Gordon on drums. He wrote the music himself, the lyrics were by Pete Brown.

The original plan was to call it Into the Storm, but when taking photographs in Scotland he found no stormy weather. The cover therefore shows him in a small wood. The album was well received, by Allan Jones of Melody Maker among others, but sold poorly. On the Billboard chart it reached number 160.
werk/jack-bruce-out-of-the-storm.listen: Listen to Pieces of Mind, the opening track, and notice how Bruce takes the lead as singer and bassist.

werk/jack-bruce-songs-for-a-tailor.text:
Songs for a Tailor was released in September 1969, shortly after Cream broke up. It was the first Jack Bruce solo album to come out. The title is a tribute to Jeannie Franklyn, Cream's clothes designer, who was killed in a car accident two days before his twenty-sixth birthday. The lyrics were written by the poet Pete Brown. Most of the tracks revolve around Bruce, the guitarist Chris Spedding and the drummer Jon Hiseman, who were given no arrangements and worked out for themselves what fitted. On Never Tell Your Mother She's Out of Tune, George Harrison plays guitar.

The record reached number 6 on the British album chart. Rolling Stone found it a disappointment on release, but later critics wrote with great praise, and the BBC called it groundbreaking. Pete Brown's literary lyrics remain controversial. Theme for an Imaginary Western, famously covered by Mountain, is regarded as the best-known track.
werk/jack-bruce-songs-for-a-tailor.listen: Listen to Theme for an Imaginary Western and notice the roots-flavoured sound, with layered piano and organ and a rhythm section that rolls calmly along.

werk/jack-bruce-things-we-like.text:
Things We Like is Jack Bruce's only instrumental album. He recorded it in August 1968, while he was still playing with Cream, but it did not come out until late 1970, a year after Songs for a Tailor. It thus became his second solo album to appear, but the first to be recorded. Bruce is said to have written most of the pieces as early as 1955, when he was twelve.

Unlike his rock and blues records, this is a jazz album, drawing on the bebop of the 1950s and the free jazz of the 1960s. Bruce plays mostly double bass, an instrument he rarely recorded. He works with the saxophonist Dick Heckstall-Smith and the guitarist John McLaughlin, with whom he had previously played in Graham Bond's band. HCKHH Blues had already been recorded live in 1963 by the Graham Bond Quartet. The record did not chart on release.
werk/jack-bruce-things-we-like.listen: Listen to Things We Like and notice the double bass: Bruce plays an instrument here that he rarely recorded.

werk/jack-dejohnette-new-directions.text:
New Directions is a 1978 album by Jack DeJohnette, recorded in June and released shortly afterwards by ECM. The group is a quartet: DeJohnette himself on drums and piano, the trumpeter Lester Bowie, the guitarist John Abercrombie and the bassist Eddie Gomez. Manfred Eicher produced, Jan Erik Kongshaug engineered. Two tracks, Dream Stalker and One Handed Woman, were written jointly by the whole band.

Reactions varied. DownBeat called it a deeply satisfying album that swings in its own wandering yet sharp way. AllMusic found the music somewhat dull because of its heavy use of space, with less trumpet and humour from Bowie than hoped for, but named strong moments from Abercrombie and DeJohnette.
werk/jack-dejohnette-new-directions.listen: Listen to Bayou Fever and notice how the four musicians leave space between the notes.

werk/jack-dejohnette-pictures.text:
Pictures is an album by the American jazz drummer and composer Jack DeJohnette. He recorded it in February 1976, and it was released a year later on ECM. Remarkably, he plays more than just drums himself: the piano and organ are his too. Only on Pictures 3 to 5 does the guitarist John Abercrombie join in as a guest, on electric and acoustic guitar.

Manfred Eicher produced, Jan Erik Kongshaug was the sound engineer, and the photographs on the cover are by Roberto Masotti. The tracks have no titles but only a number, from Picture 1 to Picture 6. Reception was moderate: AllMusic gave the album two and a half stars.
werk/jack-dejohnette-pictures.listen: Listen to Picture 3, where John Abercrombie's guitar joins in, and notice how it relates to the drums.
